e.t: This word means “to indulge” or “to live in pleasure.” It describes giving oneself over to enjoyment, especially a pleasure-seeking way of life rather than restrained living. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Timothy 5:6 and James 5:5. These occurrences place the word in settings where pleasure is treated as a dominant pursuit. Its basic sense is not merely that someone experiences happiness, but that a person lives for pleasure or freely gives themselves to it. The surrounding verse supplies the specific force in each passage.

e.t: This word means “testifies with” or “to testify with”: it describes giving confirming testimony alongside another witness or truth. It expresses agreement in bearing witness, rather than merely speaking or making a claim. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Romans, and is rendered with the idea of testifying or testifying together. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what person or truth is being confirmed there. [p03:word:greek-nt:G4828:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G4828:occurrences]

e.t: This word means “fellow soldier,” referring to someone who serves alongside another in shared work or struggle. It presents the person as a comrade and partner rather than as a distant associate. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Philippians 2:25 and Philemon 1:2. Its basic sense is therefore one of companionship in committed service, while the surrounding verse determines how that shared service is being described.

e.t: This Greek New Testament adjective means “wretched”: it describes someone in a miserable, pitiable condition. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Romans and once in Revelation. In both places, it functions as a direct description of a person rather than naming an action or object. The surrounding verse determines what kind of misery is being described, so its central sense remains a sober expression of wretchedness.

e.t: This word means to praise God by singing hymns or sacred songs. It describes vocal worship offered in song, joining honor toward God with musical expression. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each referring to the act of singing praise. Its central idea is therefore worship expressed through a hymn or sacred song, whether sung by one person or a gathered community. The surrounding verse determines who is singing and what occasion prompts the praise.

e.t: This word means “kindness”: a gracious, benevolent quality expressed toward others. It describes goodness that is considerate and helpful rather than harsh or self-seeking. In the New Testament, it is associated with God’s gracious dealings and with the character believers are to display. It also appears among the qualities produced by the Spirit. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek New Testament, showing a recurring emphasis on kindness as both something received and something practiced.
